title: Recall: questions, flashcards, misconceptions, predictions, explain-back

blocks.q: Which of the following is TRUE?
options: Every relation in 3NF is also in BCNF
A relation R is in 3NF if every non-prime attribute of R is fully functionally dependent on every key of R
Every relation in BCNF is also in 3NF
No relation can be in both BCNF and 3NF
blocks.explain: BCNF demands the LHS of every non-trivial FD be a superkey; 3NF also accepts FDs whose RHS is prime. So BCNF ⊂ 3NF. Option B is the definition of **2NF**, not 3NF.

blocks.q: Which properties does **strict two-phase locking** guarantee for every schedule it allows?
blocks.explain: 2PL gives conflict serializability. Holding exclusive locks until commit means nobody reads uncommitted data, so schedules are cascadeless and therefore recoverable. Deadlock is still possible: T1 locks A and waits for B while T2 locks B and waits for A.

blocks.q: The maximum number of superkeys for the relation schema R(E, F, G, H) with E as the key is ____.
blocks.explain: Every superkey must contain E; each of F, G, H is independently in or out: 2³ = **8**.

blocks.q: Arrange the clauses in **logical** processing order (the order the engine evaluates them, not the order you type them).
blocks.explain: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. That is why a column alias defined in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE but can be used in ORDER BY.

blocks.q: Match each read phenomenon to the **weakest** ANSI isolation level that rules it out.
blocks.explain: Each ANSI level forbids one more phenomenon: READ COMMITTED stops dirty reads, REPEATABLE READ also stops non-repeatable reads, SERIALIZABLE also stops phantoms.

source.ref: ANSI SQL-92 isolation levels; Korth 7e, ch. 17

cards.back: A set of attributes whose values uniquely identify a tuple in every legal instance of the relation.
A **minimal** superkey: remove any attribute and it stops being a superkey.
An attribute that belongs to at least one candidate key.
Attributes in one relation whose values must appear as the primary key of the referenced relation (or be NULL).
T1 reads a value written by T2 that T2 has not yet committed.
T1 reads the same row twice and gets different values because T2 updated and committed in between.
T1 re-runs a predicate query and sees a different set of rows because T2 inserted or deleted matching rows.
T1 and T2 both read a value, both write a new one, and the later write silently overwrites the earlier.

blocks.claim: `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(column)` always return the same number.
blocks.refutation: `COUNT(column)` counts only rows where that column is **not NULL**. `COUNT(*)` counts rows.
blocks.correctModel: Every aggregate except `COUNT(*)` ignores NULLs. `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` ignores NULLs too.

blocks.claim: `WHERE x = NULL` finds the rows where x is NULL.
blocks.cue: This is false, and it fails silently.
blocks.refutation: Any comparison with NULL evaluates to **UNKNOWN**, not TRUE. `WHERE` keeps only rows whose condition is TRUE, so `x = NULL` returns no rows at all.
blocks.correctModel: Use `x IS NULL` / `x IS NOT NULL`. SQL uses three-valued logic: TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN.

blocks.claim: A relation in 3NF is automatically in BCNF.
blocks.refutation: 3NF allows an FD X → A whose LHS is not a superkey **as long as A is prime**. BCNF allows no such exception.
blocks.correctModel: BCNF ⊂ 3NF. The gap is exactly the FDs with a non-superkey LHS and a prime RHS.

evidence.title: R(A, B, C), F = { AB → C, C → B }; candidate keys AB, AC

blocks.prompt: How many rows does this query return?

given.sql:
SELECT e.name, d.dname
FROM emp e
LEFT JOIN dept d ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
WHERE d.dname <> 'Sales';

reveal.title: LEFT JOIN result, then WHERE d.dname <> 'Sales'

reveal.md: A `WHERE` filter on the right table of a LEFT JOIN throws away the NULL-extended rows, turning it into an inner join. Put the condition in `ON`, or write `d.dname IS DISTINCT FROM 'Sales'`.

given.text: Same `emp` and `dept` tables as above: `emp.dept_id` holds 10, 20, NULL, 10.

reveal.md: `30 NOT IN (10, 20, NULL, 10)` means `30 <> 10 AND 30 <> 20 AND 30 <> NULL AND ...`. The `30 <> NULL` term is UNKNOWN, so the whole AND is UNKNOWN and the row is dropped. One NULL in the subquery empties the result.
Use `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM emp e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id)`: it returns **Ops** as intended.

blocks.prompt: Under READ COMMITTED, which anomaly does this schedule show?

reveal.md: T1 read the same item twice inside one transaction and saw two different committed values: a **non-repeatable read**. READ COMMITTED allows it; REPEATABLE READ forbids it.

blocks.prompt: Explain why every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but not every 3NF relation is in BCNF. Give an example.

rubric.point: States BCNF: for every non-trivial FD X → Y, X is a superkey
States 3NF's extra escape: each attribute of Y − X may instead be prime (part of some candidate key)
Gives a 3NF-but-not-BCNF example, e.g. R(A,B,C) with AB → C, C → B

blocks.modelAnswer: BCNF requires that for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y, X is a superkey. 3NF accepts the same FDs plus one escape: an FD is also fine if every attribute in Y − X is a prime attribute (belongs to some candidate key). Any relation meeting the stricter BCNF condition therefore meets 3NF. The converse fails: R(A, B, C) with AB → C and C → B has candidate keys AB and AC. C → B has a non-superkey LHS, so R is not in BCNF, but B is prime, so R is in 3NF.

blocks.prompt: Why does **strict** 2PL avoid cascading rollbacks when basic 2PL does not?
blocks.modelAnswer: Strict 2PL holds every exclusive lock until the transaction commits or aborts. No other transaction can read a value it wrote until that value is committed, so there are no dirty reads. If the writer aborts, nobody depended on its data, so no other transaction has to roll back with it: schedules are cascadeless. Basic 2PL may release an exclusive lock in its shrinking phase before commit, letting another transaction read uncommitted data and forcing a cascade if the writer later aborts.
